stimuli.title: The Four O'Clock Shift
stimuli.text:
The alarm went off at a quarter to four, and for a moment Priya could not remember why she had set it. Then she smelt it, even through the bedroom wall: yeast, warm and sour, the smell of her grandmother's bakery waking up below the flat.

She had begged for this for a year. Every school holiday she had asked, and every time Nani had laughed and said, "When your hands are ready." Priya had never understood what that meant. Her hands were the same as anyone's.

Downstairs, the kitchen was bright and loud with the hum of the ovens. Nani did not look up. She was folding a great pale mound of dough, lifting the edge and pressing it into the middle, turning it a quarter, lifting again. Her forearms were dusted white to the elbow.

"Wash," she said. "Then watch."

Priya watched for an hour. She watched the dough being cut and weighed, each piece dropped on the scale and corrected with a pinch, never more than twice. She watched loaves being shaped with three quick movements that she could not follow, no matter how closely she looked. When at last Nani slid a piece of dough across the bench to her, Priya pressed it, rolled it, folded it, and produced something that looked like a sleeping cat that had been sat on.

She waited for the laugh. It did not come.

"Again," said Nani.

By six o'clock Priya had made eleven sleeping cats. The twelfth was almost round. Nani picked it up, turned it over, and put it on the tray with the others, the real ones, the ones that would be sold.

Priya stared at it as the tray went into the oven. Her shoulders ached and there was dough under every fingernail. She looked down at her hands, and for the first time they did not seem quite the same as anyone's.

stimuli.title: The Bird That Borrows Every Song
stimuli.text:
Walk through the wet mountain forests east of Melbourne on a winter morning and you may hear a kookaburra laugh, a whipbird crack its whip and a rosella chatter, all from the same patch of ferns. Look closely, and you may find that every one of those calls is coming from a single brown bird about the size of a pheasant. This is the superb lyrebird, and it is one of the finest mimics in the animal world.

Male lyrebirds do most of the singing. During the breeding season, which falls in the cold months, each male clears a small mound of earth on the forest floor and performs on it, sometimes for hours a day. He throws his long tail forward over his head so that its fine, lacy feathers form a shimmering canopy, then pours out a stream of sounds copied from the birds around him. A good performance can contain the calls of a dozen or more species, delivered so accurately that it can be hard to tell the copy from the real bird.

Why go to so much trouble? Researchers believe the song is aimed mainly at females, who move between the mounds and listen. A male who can copy many species, and copy them well, may be showing that he is old enough and healthy enough to have spent years learning. In other words, the song is a kind of advertisement.

Lyrebirds are also known for copying sounds that are not made by birds at all. Stories of birds imitating car alarms, camera shutters and chainsaws are often repeated, and some have been recorded, mostly from birds living close to people. Scientists point out that these cases are unusual. In the wild, most of a lyrebird's song is made of the forest's own voices.

That makes the lyrebird a living record of its surroundings. If a forest falls silent, so, in time, does part of the lyrebird's song.

stimuli.title: Late Train
stimuli.text:
The last train home is mostly empty seats
and windows black as water. In the glass
the carriage floats beside us, and repeats
each yellow light we never seem to pass.

A woman in a nurse's coat is sleeping
upright, her bag held tightly on her knee.
A boy in football socks is keeping
score on a phone of games no one will see.

And I am in the window too, a pale
and borrowed face that rides along outside,
that leans its head against the rattling rail
and goes wherever I go, for the ride.

The doors breathe open. Nobody gets on.
The station's clock is wrong. And then it's gone.

stimuli.title: Open the Library on Sundays
stimuli.text:
To the editor,

Our town library is open six days a week and closed on the one day most families are actually free. I am writing to ask the council to change that.

The council will say that Sunday opening costs money, and it does. Staff must be paid, and the building must be heated and lit. But consider what we already pay for: a modern building, thousands of books, twenty computers and a quiet study room, all of it locked up for one day in seven. Opening on Sunday would not mean buying anything new. It would mean using what we have.

The people who would gain most are the people with the fewest other options. Many students in our town share small homes with large families and have no quiet place to work. Many adults work long hours from Monday to Saturday and can only visit on their day off. For them, a library closed on Sunday is a library that might as well not exist.

Some will argue that people can borrow books online now. That is true, and the online service is excellent. But a library is not only a place that lends books. It is somewhere to sit for an afternoon without being asked to buy anything. There are very few such places left.

Other councils in our region have trialled Sunday opening and kept it. I am not asking our council to promise the same. I am asking it to try: open from noon until five for six months, count the visitors, and then decide.

Yours sincerely,
D. Nguyen

stimuli.title: The Audition
stimuli.text:
Theo had practised the piece so many times that he could play it in his sleep, and some nights he did, his fingers twitching on the blanket. But the hall at the conservatorium was nothing like his bedroom. It was enormous and cold, and the piano at the front of it was so black and shiny that he could see his own nervous face in its lid.

There were three judges behind a long table. The one in the middle had silver hair and did not smile. She wrote something before Theo had played a note, and he spent a frantic second wondering what it could be. Had he walked wrongly? Was his shirt untucked?

He sat. He adjusted the stool, then adjusted it back. He put his hands on the keys and the first bars came out clean and bright, exactly as they had at home. Then, in the ninth bar, his left hand slipped. It was only one note, but in that great quiet room it rang out like a dropped saucepan.

Theo felt his face burn. Every instinct told him to stop, to apologise, to start again. Instead, he heard his teacher's voice, as clearly as if she were standing beside him: "The audience only remembers what you do next."

So he kept going. He played the slow middle section more gently than he ever had before, because his hands were still shaking and gentleness was all they could manage. And somewhere in that section, the shaking stopped.

When he finished, the silver-haired judge looked up for the first time. "The middle," she said. "Where did that come from?"

Theo opened his mouth and found he had no answer at all.

stimuli.title: A Road Built as a Memorial
stimuli.text:
The Great Ocean Road winds for about 240 kilometres along the south-west coast of Victoria, between Torquay and Allansford. Today it is one of the most famous drives in Australia, crowded with tourists who come for its cliffs, beaches and limestone stacks. But the road was not built for tourism alone. It was built as a memorial, and it was built by people who had come home from war.

At the end of the First World War, thousands of Australian soldiers returned to a country that struggled to find work for them. At the same time, the coastal towns of south-west Victoria were cut off from one another, reachable only by sea or by rough bush tracks. A plan was formed to solve both problems at once: returned servicemen would be employed to build a road along the coast, and the road would honour those who had died in the war.

Work began in 1919. Around three thousand returned soldiers worked on the road over the following years, much of it by hand. They used picks, shovels, wheelbarrows and explosives to cut a path into steep cliffs above the sea. The work was dangerous, and some workers lost their lives. The camps were basic, and the men endured cold winds and heavy rain.

The road opened in stages, and the full route was officially opened in 1932. For some years drivers paid a toll to use it, which helped repay the cost of building it.

The Great Ocean Road is often described as the world's largest war memorial. Unlike a statue or a plaque, it is a memorial that people use every day, and most of those who drive it never realise what it commemorates.

stimuli.title: Grandfather's Shed
stimuli.text:
It smells of oil and sawdust and of rain
that came in under the door one year, and stayed.
The tools hang on their nails in a neat chain
of outlines, drawn in marker, where they're laid.

He drew around each one so he would know
which one was missing, and who had it, and why.
The outlines stay. The tools began to go
to cousins, neighbours, friends. I don't know why

I keep coming here. There's nothing left to mend.
The bench is clear. The radio is still.
But every empty outline, end to end,
is shaped exactly like the thing it held,

and in the dust the light makes on the floor
I see his hands, and what the tools were for.

stimuli.title: Two Views on the Skate Park
stimuli.text:
Text 1: from a letter by a local resident

The proposal to build a skate park in Riverside Reserve is well meant, but the reserve is the wrong place for it. Riverside is one of the few quiet green spaces left in our suburb. Older residents walk there every morning, and parents bring small children to the playground because it is calm. A skate park would bring noise from early morning until after dark, and the car park, which is already full on weekends, cannot cope with more visitors. I am not against young people having somewhere to skate. I am against putting it where it will spoil the reserve for everyone else.

Text 2: from a speech by a Year 10 student to the council

Every week, police move skaters on from the shopping centre car park, the library steps and the train station. We are told, again and again, that we cannot skate there. Fine. Then tell us where we can. Riverside Reserve is close to the station and to two schools, so young people could get there without being driven. It is open and easy to see from the road, which makes it safer than the empty car parks where people skate now. A skate park is not a nuisance being forced on a community. It is part of the community making room for us.

stimuli.title: How Bees Keep Their Cool
stimuli.text:
A honey bee colony is in some ways a single animal. Tens of thousands of bees share one nest, and together they control the conditions inside it with remarkable precision. Nowhere is this clearer than in the way they manage temperature.

The young bees, or brood, develop properly only within a narrow range of warmth, about 34 to 35 degrees Celsius. If the brood is too cold, the bees are slow to develop; if it is too hot, they may be damaged or die. The colony therefore works hard to keep the brood area steady, whatever the weather outside.

On a cold day, worker bees cluster tightly and shiver their flight muscles without moving their wings. This releases heat, rather as people shiver when they are cold. On a hot day, the problem is reversed, and the colony has several ways to deal with it.

First, some workers line up at the entrance and fan their wings, drawing air through the nest. Second, foragers that would normally collect nectar begin collecting water instead. They spread tiny droplets over the comb, and as the water evaporates, it carries heat away, cooling the nest in much the same way that sweat cools skin. Third, when the nest becomes very crowded and warm, many bees may leave the comb and hang in a cluster outside the entrance, which reduces the heat produced inside.

No single bee directs any of this. Each worker responds to the conditions immediately around her, and the colony's temperature control emerges from thousands of small decisions.

stimuli.title: Lost at the Show
stimuli.text:
Mai had been holding her little brother's hand for the entire afternoon, through the animal pavilion and the woodchop and the long, sticky queue for fairy floss. She let go for exactly ten seconds to pay for a showbag. When she turned around, Bao was gone.

For a moment the crowd seemed to grow louder and taller, a wall of legs and prams and elbows. Mai's first thought was to run, anywhere, calling his name. Her second thought, which arrived a heartbeat later and in her mother's voice, was: stop, and think like Bao.

Bao was five. Bao did not care about showbags or woodchopping. Bao had spent the whole day talking about one thing, and he had talked about it so often that Mai had stopped listening.

The tractors.

She pushed back through the crowd towards the farm machinery display, past the dog trial and the jam judging, and there he was, standing on the bottom step of an enormous green tractor, staring up at the cabin as if it were a castle. He had not even noticed he was lost.

Mai's legs, she discovered, had gone wobbly. She sat down on the grass beside the tractor and waited until they felt like legs again.

"Can I go up?" said Bao.

"No," said Mai. Then, because her heart was still thumping and she had never been so glad to see anyone in her life, she said, "Maybe. Let's find someone to ask."

questions.stem: What is the value of −7 − (−12) + 3 × (−2)?
A school has 720 students and 45% of them walk to school. How many students do not walk to school?
questions.explanation: 55% do not walk. 10% of 720 is 72, so 50% is 360 and 5% is 36: 360 + 36 = 396. 324 is the number who do walk.

questions.stem: Solve 7x − 5 = 3x + 19.
questions.explanation: Subtract 3x from both sides: 4x − 5 = 19. Add 5: 4x = 24, so x = 6. Check: 7(6) − 5 = 37 and 3(6) + 19 = 37.

questions.stem: A train travels 225 km in 2 hours 30 minutes. What is its average speed?
questions.explanation: 2 hours 30 minutes is 2.5 hours, and 225 ÷ 2.5 = 90 km/h. 112.5 km/h comes from dividing by 2, and 75 km/h from treating 30 minutes as 1 hour.

questions.stem: A bag holds 4 red, 6 blue and 5 green marbles. One marble is taken at random. What is the probability that it is not blue?
questions.explanation: There are 15 marbles and 4 + 5 = 9 are not blue, so the probability is 9/15 = 3/5. 2/5 is the chance it is blue.

questions.stem: What is the median of 7, 3, 9, 4, 12 and 8?
questions.explanation: In order: 3, 4, 7, 8, 9, 12. With six numbers the median is halfway between the middle two, 7 and 8, so 7.5. 6.5 comes from using 9 and 4 without sorting.
Divide first: 3/4 ÷ 3/2 = 3/4 × 2/3 = 1/2. Then 2/3 + 1/2 = 4/6 + 3/6 = 7/6. 17/18 comes from adding before dividing.

questions.stem: Green paint is made by mixing blue and yellow paint in the ratio 3 : 5. How much blue paint is needed to make 12 litres of green paint?
questions.explanation: There are 3 + 5 = 8 parts, so one part is 12 ÷ 8 = 1.5 litres. Blue is 3 parts: 3 × 1.5 = 4.5 litres. 7.5 litres is the yellow paint.

questions.stem: What is the value of 2⁵ × 2³ ÷ 2⁴?
questions.explanation: Add the powers when multiplying and subtract when dividing: 5 + 3 − 4 = 4, and 2⁴ = 16.

questions.stem: Which expression is equal to 3(2x − 5) − 2(x − 4)?
questions.explanation: 3(2x − 5) = 6x − 15 and −2(x − 4) = −2x + 8. Together: 6x − 2x − 15 + 8 = 4x − 7. 4x − 23 comes from writing −2 × −4 as −8.

questions.stem: A trapezium has parallel sides of 9 cm and 15 cm, and a perpendicular height of 8 cm. What is its area?
questions.explanation: Area = half the sum of the parallel sides × height = (9 + 15) ÷ 2 × 8 = 12 × 8 = 96 cm². 192 cm² forgets to halve.

questions.stem: Using π ≈ 22/7, what is the circumference of a circle with a radius of 7 cm?
questions.explanation: Circumference = 2πr = 2 × 22/7 × 7 = 44 cm. 154 cm is the number you get for the area, πr², and 22 cm uses the radius instead of the diameter.

questions.stem: The three angles of a triangle are in the ratio 3 : 4 : 5. What is the size of the largest angle?
questions.explanation: The angles add to 180° and there are 3 + 4 + 5 = 12 parts, so one part is 15°. The largest is 5 × 15° = 75°.

questions.stem: A container shaped like a rectangular prism measures 12 cm by 5 cm by 4 cm on the inside. How much water does it hold when full? (1 cm³ = 1 mL)
questions.explanation: Volume = 12 × 5 × 4 = 240 cm³, and 1 cm³ holds 1 mL, so it holds 240 mL. 2.4 L would be 2400 mL, ten times too much, and 120 mL halves the volume.

questions.stem: The mean of five numbers is 14. Four of the numbers are 10, 12, 15 and 18. What is the fifth number?
questions.explanation: Five numbers with a mean of 14 add to 5 × 14 = 70. The four given add to 55, so the fifth is 70 − 55 = 15.

questions.stem: In a table of values, x = 1, 2, 3, 4 gives y = 5, 8, 11, 14. Which rule fits the table?
questions.explanation: y goes up by 3 each time x goes up by 1, so the rule is y = 3x + c. When x = 1, y = 5, so c = 2. y = x + 4 works only for the first pair.

questions.stem: If a = −3 and b = 4, what is the value of a² − 2ab?
questions.explanation: a² = (−3)² = 9 and 2ab = 2 × (−3) × 4 = −24. So 9 − (−24) = 33. 15 comes from treating (−3)² as −9, and −15 from subtracting 24 instead of −24.

questions.stem: The price of a book rose from \$40 to \$50. What was the percentage increase?
questions.explanation: The increase is \$10 on an original \$40, and 10/40 = 25%. 20% divides by the new price instead of the original.

questions.stem: Each exterior angle of a regular polygon is 30°. How many sides does the polygon have?
questions.explanation: The exterior angles of any polygon add to 360°, so a regular polygon with 30° exterior angles has 360 ÷ 30 = 12 sides.

questions.stem: A park has an area of 3.5 hectares. What is this in square metres? (1 hectare = 10 000 m²)
questions.explanation: Multiply by 10 000: 3.5 × 10 000 = 35 000 m². A hectare is a square 100 m by 100 m.

questions.stem: What number comes next? 3, 7, 15, 31, 63, ...
questions.explanation: Each number is double the one before, plus 1: 63 × 2 + 1 = 127. The gaps also double (4, 8, 16, 32, 64).

questions.stem: A number machine multiplies a number by 3 and then subtracts 4. The output is 29. What was the input?
questions.explanation: Work backwards and undo each step in reverse order: 29 + 4 = 33, then 33 ÷ 3 = 11. 83 runs the machine forwards on 29.

questions.stem: What number goes in the box? 7 × ☐ − 8 = 48
questions.explanation: Undo the subtraction first: 48 + 8 = 56. Then 56 ÷ 7 = 8.

questions.stem: Three consecutive even numbers add up to 96. What is the largest of them?
questions.explanation: The middle number is 96 ÷ 3 = 32, so the numbers are 30, 32 and 34.

questions.stem: The pattern 1/2, 2/3, 3/4, 4/5, ... continues. What is the 10th fraction?
questions.explanation: The nth fraction is n/(n + 1), so the 10th is 10/11. 9/10 is the 9th.

questions.stem: What number comes next? 2, 3, 5, 9, 17, ...
questions.explanation: The gaps are 1, 2, 4, 8, so the next gap is 16: 17 + 16 = 33. 25 repeats the last gap of 8.

questions.stem: What number comes next? 50, 45, 47, 42, 44, ...
questions.explanation: The pattern alternates: subtract 5, add 2. After 44 comes 44 − 5 = 39.

questions.stem: The symbol ★ means a ★ b = 2a − b. What is the value of 5 ★ (3 ★ 1)?
questions.explanation: Work out the brackets first: 3 ★ 1 = 2 × 3 − 1 = 5. Then 5 ★ 5 = 2 × 5 − 5 = 5.

questions.stem: 3 apples weigh the same as 2 pears, and 4 pears weigh the same as 6 bananas. How many bananas weigh the same as 6 apples?
questions.explanation: 6 apples weigh the same as 4 pears (double 3 apples = 2 pears), and 4 pears weigh the same as 6 bananas. So 6 apples balance 6 bananas.

questions.stem:
Each row of the table follows the same rule. What is the missing number?

| First | Second | Third |
|---|---|---|
| 2 | 5 | 11 |
| 3 | 7 | 15 |
| 4 | ? | 19 |
questions.explanation: In each row, double a number and add 1 to get the next: 2 → 5 → 11 and 3 → 7 → 15. So 4 → 9 → 19, which checks with the 19 given.

questions.stem: A clock gains 4 minutes every hour. It is set to the correct time at 8:00 am. What time does it show when the correct time is 2:30 pm?
questions.explanation: From 8:00 am to 2:30 pm is 6.5 hours, so the clock gains 6.5 × 4 = 26 minutes. It shows 2:30 + 26 minutes = 2:56 pm. 2:54 pm counts only 6 hours.

questions.stem: How many two-digit numbers have digits that add up to 9?
questions.explanation: They are 18, 27, 36, 45, 54, 63, 72, 81 and 90. 09 is not a two-digit number, so there are 9.

questions.stem: A row of squares is made from matchsticks, with neighbouring squares sharing a side. 1 square uses 4 matchsticks, 2 squares use 7 and 3 squares use 10. How many matchsticks are needed for 20 squares?
questions.explanation: The first square uses 4 and each extra square adds 3, so 20 squares use 4 + 19 × 3 = 61. 80 would be 20 separate squares.

questions.stem: Each letter is worth its place in the alphabet: A = 1, B = 2, C = 3 and so on, and a word is worth the sum of its letters. Which word is worth 20?
Which two signs make this true? 12 ☐ 3 ☐ 2 = 8
The same rule turns the first two numbers in each group into the third: (4, 5, 21), (3, 7, 22), (6, 2, ?). What is the missing number?
questions.explanation: Multiply the first two numbers and add 1: 4 × 5 + 1 = 21 and 3 × 7 + 1 = 22, so 6 × 2 + 1 = 13.

questions.stem: Ana is three times as old as Ben. In six years' time she will be twice as old as he is. How old is Ana now?
questions.explanation: If Ben is b, Ana is 3b. In six years: 3b + 6 = 2(b + 6), so 3b + 6 = 2b + 12 and b = 6. Ana is 18. Check: in six years they are 24 and 12.

questions.stem: Jo has 20 coins, all of them 20c or 50c coins. Together they are worth \$7.60. How many 50c coins does Jo have?
questions.explanation: If all 20 were 20c coins they would be worth \$4.00. Each swap to a 50c coin adds 30c, and \$3.60 ÷ 30c = 12. Check: 12 × 50c + 8 × 20c = \$6.00 + \$1.60 = \$7.60.

questions.stem: The average of A and B is 30, the average of B and C is 40, and the average of A and C is 35. What is B?
questions.explanation: So A + B = 60, B + C = 80 and A + C = 70. Adding all three: 2(A + B + C) = 210, so A + B + C = 105. B = 105 − 70 = 35.

questions.stem: Pipe A fills a tank in 6 hours and pipe B fills it in 3 hours. How long do they take to fill the empty tank together?
questions.explanation: In one hour A fills 1/6 and B fills 1/3 = 2/6, so together they fill 3/6 = 1/2 of the tank. The whole tank takes 2 hours. 4.5 hours averages the times, which cannot be right as two pipes are faster than either alone.

questions.stem: Why had Nani always told Priya to wait "when your hands are ready"?
options: She believed baking skill had to be learned through practice
She thought Priya's hands were too small for the dough
She did not want Priya to get up so early
She wanted Priya to finish school before working
questions.explanation: By the end Priya's hands have learned something through hours of repetition, which shows what Nani meant: readiness comes from practice. Nothing suggests Nani worried about size, early starts or school.

questions.stem: Each piece of dough was "corrected with a pinch". This means Nani
options: squeezed the dough to help it rise
added a pinch of salt for flavour
adjusted the weight with a little dough
pinched Priya to correct her mistakes
questions.explanation: The pieces are being cut and weighed on a scale, so a pinch corrects the weight. The sentence is about the dough, not Priya.

questions.stem: Priya's first attempts are described as looking like "a sleeping cat that had been sat on". The writer uses this image mainly to
options: suggest that Priya would rather be back in bed
show, with humour, how lumpy her loaves were
show that Priya was careless with the dough
hint that a cat lived in the bakery
questions.explanation: The comparison is a funny picture of a shapeless, squashed loaf. Priya is trying hard, so careless does not fit.

questions.stem: "She waited for the laugh. It did not come." What does this moment show about Nani?
options: She is too busy to notice the loaf
She is disappointed in Priya's work
She has lost her usual sense of humour
questions.explanation: Nani used to laugh off Priya's requests, but now that Priya is working she simply says "Again", treating her as a learner. Nothing suggests disappointment or that she failed to notice.

questions.stem: Which sentence best expresses the main idea of the story?
options: Grandparents are stricter teachers than parents are
Getting up early is the real secret to success
Skill comes slowly through effort, and brings pride
Baking bread is too difficult for most children
questions.explanation: The story moves from failed loaves to one good enough to sell, and ends with Priya seeing her hands differently. The other options take a small detail or contradict the ending.

questions.stem: What is the passage mainly about?
options: How and why the superb lyrebird copies other sounds
Where to see birds in the forests near Melbourne
Why lyrebirds copy chainsaws and car alarms
questions.explanation: Every paragraph is about the lyrebird's mimicry: what it sounds like, why males do it and what it copies. Chainsaws are only one unusual detail.

questions.stem: According to the passage, when do male lyrebirds perform on their mounds?
options: Only at dawn during the summer months
All year round, at any time of day
In the breeding season, in the cold months
questions.explanation: The second paragraph says the breeding season "falls in the cold months", and that is when each male performs on his mound.

questions.stem: Why might a female lyrebird prefer a male who copies many species well?
options: It frightens rival males away from his mound
It suggests he has lived and learned for years
It attracts insects that she can feed on
It shows that he lives close to people
questions.explanation: The passage says a skilled mimic may be showing he is "old enough and healthy enough to have spent years learning". The other reasons are not mentioned.

questions.stem: Why does the writer include the sentence "Scientists point out that these cases are unusual"?
options: To balance the famous stories with what is usual
To show that the famous stories are made up
To warn readers not to record lyrebirds at home
To prove lyrebirds prefer machine sounds
questions.explanation: The writer accepts that some cases were recorded but stresses that wild lyrebirds mostly copy the forest. So the sentence keeps the unusual stories in proportion rather than calling them false.

questions.stem: The last sentence says that if a forest falls silent, "so, in time, does part of the lyrebird's song". What does this suggest?
options: Lyrebirds stop singing altogether in the winter
Lyrebirds sing only when the forest is noisy
Lyrebirds can only copy birds that are still around
Logging machines frighten lyrebirds into silence
questions.explanation: The song is a "living record" of the birds around it. If those birds vanish, young lyrebirds have nothing to copy, so that part of the song is lost over time.

questions.stem: When is the poem set?
options: In the middle of the day
questions.explanation: It is "the last train home", the windows are "black as water" and a nurse is asleep, all of which point to late at night.

questions.stem: In the first verse, why does the carriage seem to float "beside us"?
options: The train is crossing a river
Its reflection appears in the dark window
questions.explanation: "In the glass" the carriage is repeated, which is a reflection in a window made dark by the night outside.

questions.stem: What can the reader most likely infer about the woman in the nurse's coat?
options: She is going to a party
She is afraid of the boy
questions.explanation: She is asleep upright in a nurse's coat on the last train home, so she is very tired, probably after a long shift. Nothing in the poem says she missed her stop or fears anyone.

questions.stem: The speaker calls the face in the window "borrowed". This suggests the face
options: will be given back at the end of the trip
has been painted onto the glass
questions.explanation: The "pale and borrowed face" goes wherever the speaker goes, so it is the speaker's own reflection, borrowed from the real face for a while.

questions.stem: Which word best describes the mood of the poem?
questions.explanation: The speaker calmly notices sleeping passengers, reflections and an empty station. Nothing in the poem is threatening, joyful or angry.

questions.stem: What does the writer want the council to do?
options: Build a new library with more computers
Trial opening the library on Sunday afternoons
Close the library on a weekday instead
Spend less on the online lending service
questions.explanation: The final paragraph asks the council to open "from noon until five for six months, count the visitors, and then decide".

questions.stem: How does the writer respond to the point that Sunday opening costs money?
options: By agreeing, but saying the building sits unused
By denying that it would cost anything at all
By suggesting volunteers could run the library
By saying that other councils would pay for it
questions.explanation: The writer admits "it does" cost money, then points out that the town already pays for a building and resources that sit unused one day a week.

questions.stem: Which group does the writer say would gain most from Sunday opening?
options: People with the fewest other places to go
Library staff who want extra shifts
questions.explanation: The third paragraph says "the people who would gain most are the people with the fewest other options", such as students without a quiet place at home.

questions.stem: Other councils "have trialled Sunday opening and kept it". In this sentence, trialled means
questions.explanation: A trial is a test run. The writer then asks for the same kind of test: six months, then a decision.

questions.stem: Why does the writer say "I am not asking our council to promise the same"?
options: To admit that Sunday opening has failed elsewhere
To show the writer has changed their mind
To make the request seem modest and easy to agree to
questions.explanation: By asking only for a trial rather than a permanent change, the writer makes the proposal harder to refuse. Nothing says Sunday opening failed elsewhere; the other councils kept it.

questions.stem: Glove is to hand as sock is to
questions.explanation: A glove is worn on the hand and a sock is worn on the foot. A shoe goes over a sock rather than being what the sock covers.

questions.stem: Author is to novel as composer is to
questions.explanation: An author creates a novel and a composer creates a symphony. An orchestra performs it; it is not what the composer makes.

questions.stem: Which word is closest in meaning to CANDID?
questions.explanation: Candid means open and honest about what you think, which is what frank means. Secretive is close to the opposite.

questions.stem: Which word is most nearly the opposite of SCARCE?
questions.explanation: Scarce means in short supply, so its opposite is plentiful. Rare means nearly the same as scarce, and frightened confuses it with scared.

questions.stem: Which word does not belong with the others?
questions.explanation: Kilometre, centimetre and millimetre are units of length. A litre measures volume.

questions.stem: Which word does not belong with the others?
questions.explanation: Whisper, murmur and mutter all mean speaking quietly. To shout is to speak loudly.

questions.stem: Which letter comes next? B, E, H, K, ...
questions.explanation: Each letter is three places after the one before: B (+3) E (+3) H (+3) K (+3) N.

questions.stem: In a code, FOX is written GPY. How is HEN written in the same code?
questions.explanation: Each letter moves one place forward: F→G, O→P, X→Y. So H→I, E→F and N→O gives IFO.

questions.stem: All members of the school choir can read music. Mia cannot read music. Which statement must be true?
options: Mia is not in the choir.
Everyone who reads music is in the choir.
Mia wants to join the choir.
questions.explanation: If every choir member reads music and Mia does not, she cannot be a member. Nothing is said about instruments or what Mia wants.

questions.stem: Drought is to rain as famine is to
questions.explanation: A drought is a long shortage of rain and a famine is a long shortage of food. Hunger is a result of famine, not the thing that is missing.

questions.stem: "The new evidence corroborated her story." What does corroborated mean in this sentence?
questions.explanation: To corroborate is to support or confirm with more evidence. Contradicted is the opposite.

questions.stem: Which pair comes next? AZ, BY, CX, ...
questions.explanation: The first letters go forwards through the alphabet (A, B, C, D) and the second letters go backwards from Z (Z, Y, X, W).

questions.stem: In a code, MOUSE is written ESUOM. How is PLANT written in the same code?
questions.explanation: The code writes the word backwards: MOUSE becomes ESUOM, so PLANT becomes TNALP.

questions.stem: Five friends ran a race. Ari finished ahead of Bo. Cy finished after Bo but before Dev. Eli finished ahead of Ari. There were no ties. Who finished third?
questions.explanation: Eli is ahead of Ari, who is ahead of Bo, and Cy and Dev come after Bo. The order is Eli, Ari, Bo, Cy, Dev, so Bo is third.

questions.stem: No reptiles have fur. Some pets are reptiles. Which statement must be true?
options: Some pets do not have fur.
questions.explanation: The pets that are reptiles cannot have fur, so at least some pets have none. Other pets may have fur, and the statements never say whether any reptiles are not pets.

questions.stem: Four friends sit in a row of four seats. Tia sits at one end. Uma sits next to Tia. Vic does not sit next to Uma. Who sits next to Vic?
questions.explanation: With Tia in seat 1 and Uma in seat 2, Vic cannot take seat 3 (next to Uma), so Vic is in seat 4 and Will in seat 3. Only Will sits next to Vic.

questions.stem: Which word means both "the main stem of a tree" and "a large box for storing things"?
questions.explanation: A trunk is the main stem of a tree and also a large storage box. Bark covers a tree but is not a box.

questions.stem: Which word can go in front of all three to make new words? ___ball, ___print, ___note
questions.explanation: Football, footprint and footnote are all words. Hand makes handball and handprint but not handnote, and finger makes only fingerprint.

questions.stem: Which word best completes the sentence? "Although the old bridge looked ___, engineers said it was perfectly safe."
questions.explanation: "Although" signals a contrast with "perfectly safe", so the bridge must have looked weak. Sturdy would agree with the second half instead of contrasting.

questions.stem: Thermometer is to temperature as odometer is to
questions.explanation: A thermometer measures temperature and an odometer measures the distance a vehicle has travelled. Speed is measured by a speedometer.

questions.stem: What is the value of (−4)² − 3 × (−5)?
What is 15% of 240 added to 40% of 75?
In a class, the ratio of boys to girls is 5 : 4. There are 12 girls. How many students are in the class?
questions.explanation: 4 parts = 12 girls, so 1 part = 3. The class has 5 + 4 = 9 parts, which is 27 students. 15 is just the boys.

questions.stem: Using π ≈ 3.14, what is the area of a circle with a radius of 10 cm?
questions.explanation: Area = πr² = 3.14 × 10 × 10 = 314 cm². 62.8 cm is the circumference, 2πr.

questions.stem: A film starts at 6:35 pm and runs for 2 hours 55 minutes. When does it finish?
questions.explanation: 6:35 pm plus 2 hours is 8:35 pm. Another 55 minutes: 25 minutes to 9:00 pm, then 30 more, so 9:30 pm.

questions.stem: What is the range of 4, 9, 4, 7, 12, 9, 4 and 3?
questions.explanation: Range = highest − lowest = 12 − 3 = 9. 4 is the mode, the most common value.

questions.stem: What is 3/8 written as a percentage?
questions.explanation: 3 ÷ 8 = 0.375, which is 37.5%. 38% is rounded, not exact.
Write each as an improper fraction: 3/2 × 8/3 = 24/6 = 4. 2 1/3 comes from multiplying the whole numbers and the fractions separately.

questions.stem: A \$200 jacket is reduced by 20%. Later the sale price is reduced by a further 10%. What is the final price?
questions.explanation: 20% off \$200 leaves \$160. 10% of \$160 is \$16, so the final price is \$144. \$140 wrongly takes 30% off the original price.

questions.stem: Simplify 12a²b ÷ 4ab.
questions.explanation: Divide the numbers, 12 ÷ 4 = 3, then the letters: a² ÷ a = a and b ÷ b = 1. The answer is 3a.

questions.stem: What is the size of each interior angle of a regular octagon?
questions.explanation: The interior angles of an octagon add to (8 − 2) × 180° = 1080°, and 1080° ÷ 8 = 135°. 45° is each exterior angle.

questions.stem: Six people can paint a fence in 8 hours. How long would four people take, working at the same rate?
questions.explanation: The job takes 6 × 8 = 48 person-hours. Four people need 48 ÷ 4 = 12 hours. Fewer people take longer, so any answer under 8 hours cannot be right.

questions.stem: Two fair six-sided dice are rolled. What is the probability that the two numbers add to 11?
questions.explanation: There are 36 equally likely outcomes, and 2 of them make 11: (5,6) and (6,5). 2/36 = 1/18. 1/11 wrongly treats the 11 possible totals as equally likely.

questions.stem: The mean of eight test scores is 15. A score of 22 is removed. What is the mean of the seven scores left?
questions.explanation: The eight scores add to 8 × 15 = 120. Removing 22 leaves 98, and 98 ÷ 7 = 14.

questions.stem: Which of these numbers is prime?
questions.explanation: 91 = 7 × 13, 87 = 3 × 29 and 57 = 3 × 19, but 97 has no factor other than 1 and itself.

questions.stem: A phone plan costs \$35 a month plus 10 cents for each text after the first 100. Lena sends 160 texts in a month. What is her bill?
questions.explanation: Only 160 − 100 = 60 texts are charged: 60 × 10 cents = \$6. The bill is \$35 + \$6 = \$41. \$51 charges all 160 texts.
Multiply both sides by 3: x + 4 = 6x − 21. Then 25 = 5x, so x = 5. Check: (5 + 4)/3 = 3 and 2(5) − 7 = 3. x = 11 forgets to multiply by 3.

questions.stem: A rectangular garden measures 10 m by 6 m. A 4 m by 3 m rectangle is cut out of one corner to leave an L-shape. What is the perimeter of the L-shape?
questions.explanation: Cutting a corner rectangle moves two sides inward without changing their total length, so the perimeter stays 2 × (10 + 6) = 32 m. 48 m is the area in square metres.

questions.stem: A cube has a total surface area of 150 cm². What is its volume?
questions.explanation: A cube has 6 equal faces, so each face is 150 ÷ 6 = 25 cm² and each edge is 5 cm. Volume = 5 × 5 × 5 = 125 cm³. 25 cm³ stops at the area of one face.

questions.stem: A straight line passes through the points (0, 3) and (2, 7). What is its equation?
questions.explanation: It crosses the y-axis at 3. Going from x = 0 to x = 2, y rises by 4, so the gradient is 4 ÷ 2 = 2. The line is y = 2x + 3.

questions.stem: What number comes next? 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, ...
questions.explanation: These are the square numbers 1², 2², 3², 4², 5², so next is 6² = 36. The gaps are 3, 5, 7, 9, then 11.

questions.stem: What number comes next? 96, 48, 24, 12, ...
questions.explanation: Each number is half the one before, so 12 ÷ 2 = 6.

questions.stem: A number is halved and then 7 is added. The result is 19. What was the number?
questions.explanation: Undo the steps in reverse: 19 − 7 = 12, then double: 24. 12 forgets to undo the halving.

questions.stem: A mother and her daughter have ages that add up to 50. The mother is four times as old as the daughter. How old is the daughter?
questions.explanation: The daughter is 1 part and the mother 4 parts, so 5 parts = 50 and 1 part = 10. 40 is the mother's age.

questions.stem:
Each row of the table follows the same rule. What is the missing number?

| First | Second | Third |
|---|---|---|
| 2 | 4 | 8 |
| 3 | 9 | 27 |
| 5 | ? | 125 |
questions.explanation: Each row multiplies by the first number again: 3 → 9 → 27 are 3, 3² and 3³. So the row for 5 is 5, 25, 125.

questions.stem: What number comes next? 2, 6, 12, 20, 30, ...
questions.explanation: The gaps go up by 2 each time: 4, 6, 8, 10, so the next gap is 12 and 30 + 12 = 42.

questions.stem: What number comes next? 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, ...
questions.explanation: Each number is the sum of the two before it: 5 + 8 = 13.

questions.stem: The symbol ◇ means p ◇ q = p² − q. What is the value of 3 ◇ (2 ◇ 1)?
questions.explanation: Brackets first: 2 ◇ 1 = 4 − 1 = 3. Then 3 ◇ 3 = 9 − 3 = 6.

questions.stem: A cup and a jug together weigh 900 g. Two of the same cups and the jug weigh 1.2 kg. How much does the jug weigh?
questions.explanation: The second weighing has one more cup and is 300 g heavier, so a cup weighs 300 g. The jug is 900 − 300 = 600 g.

questions.stem: In one year, 1 March is a Tuesday. What day of the week is 31 March in the same year?
questions.explanation: 31 March is 30 days after 1 March. 28 days is exactly 4 weeks, which lands on a Tuesday again (29 March), and 2 more days gives Thursday.

questions.stem: Eight people meet and every person shakes hands once with every other person. How many handshakes are there?
questions.explanation: Each of the 8 shakes 7 hands, which counts every handshake twice: 8 × 7 ÷ 2 = 28. 56 forgets to halve.

questions.stem: Two cyclists start 60 km apart and ride towards each other, one at 18 km/h and the other at 12 km/h. After how long do they meet?
questions.explanation: Together they close the gap at 18 + 12 = 30 km/h, so 60 km takes 60 ÷ 30 = 2 hours.

questions.stem: How many different ways can you make 30c using only 5c and 10c coins?
questions.explanation: Count the 10c coins: three 10c; two 10c and two 5c; one 10c and four 5c; or six 5c. That is 4 ways.

questions.stem: Using the usual order of operations, which two signs make this true? 6 ☐ 4 ☐ 2 = 22
Five friends have a mean height of 150 cm. When a sixth friend joins, the mean height becomes 152 cm. How tall is the sixth friend?
questions.explanation: The five add to 5 × 150 = 750 cm and the six to 6 × 152 = 912 cm, so the new friend is 912 − 750 = 162 cm.

questions.stem: What number comes next? 3, 20, 6, 17, 12, 14, 24, ...
questions.explanation: Two patterns take turns. The 1st, 3rd, 5th and 7th numbers double: 3, 6, 12, 24. The 2nd, 4th and 6th go down by 3: 20, 17, 14. The 8th number continues that one: 11. 48 would be the 9th.

questions.stem:
Each row of the table follows the same rule. What is the missing number?

| First | Second | Third |
|---|---|---|
| 3 | 4 | 25 |
| 5 | 12 | 169 |
| 6 | 8 | ? |
questions.explanation: The third number is the sum of the squares of the first two: 9 + 16 = 25 and 25 + 144 = 169. So 36 + 64 = 100. 196 squares the sum, 6 + 8 = 14, which does not fit the first row.

questions.stem: All the whole numbers from 1 to 100 are written down. How many times is the digit 7 written?
questions.explanation: 7 appears in the ones place in 7, 17, 27, ..., 97 (10 times) and in the tens place in 70 to 79 (10 times). 77 has two 7s and is counted in both lists, so the total is 20.

questions.stem: A two-digit number has digits that add up to 11. Reversing its digits gives a number 27 larger. What is the number?
questions.explanation: Reversing makes the number larger, so the ones digit is bigger. 47 reversed is 74, and 74 − 47 = 27. Its digits add to 11 as well. 38 reversed is 83, which is 45 larger.

questions.stem: A number is increased by 50% and the result is then decreased by 50%. The final answer is 60. What was the starting number?
questions.explanation: Increasing by 50% multiplies by 1.5 and decreasing by 50% multiplies by 0.5, so the number is multiplied by 0.75 overall. 60 ÷ 0.75 = 80. Check: 80 → 120 → 60.

questions.stem: How is the hall different from Theo's bedroom?
options: It has a better piano than his teacher's
It is huge, cold and very quiet
It is full of other students waiting
questions.explanation: The hall is "enormous and cold", and later "that great quiet room" makes one wrong note ring out.

questions.stem: Why does Theo wonder whether his shirt is untucked?
options: His nerves make him imagine criticism
He knows he got dressed in a hurry
The judge has told him to tidy himself up
He hopes to make the judges laugh
questions.explanation: The judge writes before he has played, and he "spent a frantic second" guessing why. His worries come from nerves, not from anything the judge says.

questions.stem: The wrong note rings out "like a dropped saucepan". The writer uses this comparison to show
options: that someone in the hall dropped something
that the piano was out of tune
how loud and jarring the mistake seemed to Theo
questions.explanation: A dropped saucepan makes a sudden clanging noise. The comparison shows how huge one small slip felt in the silent hall.

questions.stem: What helps Theo keep playing after his mistake?
options: Seeing the judges smile at him
questions.explanation: He hears his teacher's words, "The audience only remembers what you do next", and decides to continue rather than stop.

questions.stem: Which idea does the story most strongly suggest?
options: How you recover from a mistake matters most
Judges care only about perfect playing
questions.explanation: Theo's slip leads him to play the middle section more gently than ever, and that is what the judge notices. The story shows a recovery outshining an error.

questions.stem: What is the main purpose of the passage?
options: To persuade tourists to drive the road
To describe the beaches along the coast
To explain how and why the road was built
To argue that the road should be widened
questions.explanation: Most of the passage covers the reasons for building the road, who built it and how. The scenery is mentioned only briefly.

questions.stem: Which two problems was the road meant to solve at once?
options: Crowded tourist roads and a lack of memorials
Jobs for returned soldiers and isolated coastal towns
Rough bush tracks and expensive sea travel
questions.explanation: The second paragraph says soldiers needed work and the towns were "cut off from one another", and the road would solve "both problems at once".

questions.stem: According to the passage, when was the full route officially opened?
questions.explanation: Work began in 1919, the road opened in stages, and the full route was officially opened in 1932.

questions.stem: What does the description of picks, shovels and explosives suggest about the work?
options: It was mostly done by engineers in offices
It was hard physical labour with few machines
It was safer than other road building
questions.explanation: The writer says the road was cut "much of it by hand" with simple tools, and that the work was dangerous.

questions.stem: Why does the writer end by comparing the road with "a statue or a plaque"?
options: To show it is unusual because people use it
To suggest that statues should replace it
To complain that the road needs a plaque
To prove it is the world's largest memorial
questions.explanation: The last paragraph points out that, unlike a statue, the road is used every day, often by people who do not know what it honours. It does not try to prove the size claim, which is only reported.

questions.stem: Why did the grandfather draw around each tool?
options: To make the shed look tidy for visitors
To teach the speaker the names of tools
To decide which tools to give away
So he could tell which tool was missing
questions.explanation: The second verse says he drew around each one "so he would know which one was missing".

questions.stem: What has most likely happened to the grandfather?
options: He has moved to a new house with a bigger shed
He has died, and his tools have been given away
He has lent his tools while he is on holiday
He has stopped using the shed because of rain
questions.explanation: The tools "began to go" to relatives and friends, the bench is clear and the radio is still, and the speaker now only sees his hands in memory.

questions.stem: "The radio is still." Here, still means
questions.explanation: The radio is no longer playing, so still means silent here. It is not the "even now" meaning of still.

questions.stem: Why are the empty outlines important to the speaker?
options: They show where to hang new tools
They prove that someone stole the tools
They keep the shapes of what is gone
They were drawn by the speaker as a child
questions.explanation: Each outline is "shaped exactly like the thing it held", and looking at them the speaker sees the grandfather's hands. They are reminders of what is missing.

questions.stem: Which word best describes the speaker's feelings in the poem?
questions.explanation: The speaker keeps returning to an empty shed and remembers the grandfather's hands. The tone is sad and loving. The speaker says "I don't know why" once, but the poem is not mainly puzzled.

questions.stem: What do the two writers disagree about?
options: Whether young people should be allowed to skate
Whether the council should build a playground
Whether police should patrol the shopping centre
Whether Riverside Reserve suits a skate park
questions.explanation: The resident says "I am not against young people having somewhere to skate", so both accept skating. They disagree about the site.

questions.stem: Which reason does the resident give against the skate park?
options: The reserve is too far from the station
The car park is already full on weekends
The reserve is hard to see from the road
questions.explanation: Text 1 says the car park "is already full on weekends" and could not cope. The other points come from Text 2 or are not made.

questions.stem: How would the student most likely answer the resident's worry about extra cars?
options: Most skaters could walk from the station or school
The council should build a bigger car park
Skaters would only use the park on weekdays
Older residents could walk somewhere else
questions.explanation: The student says the reserve is close to the station and two schools, so young people "could get there without being driven", which answers the parking concern.

questions.stem: "Fine. Then tell us where we can." What is the effect of these short sentences in the student's speech?
options: They show the student agrees with the police
They move the speech on to a new topic
They make the student sound unsure and polite
They sound frustrated and challenge the council
questions.explanation: After listing places where skaters are moved on, the blunt short sentences sound frustrated and put the question back to the council.

questions.stem: The resident values the reserve because it is calm. Which point in the student's speech gives a different view of the reserve itself?
options: Skaters are moved on from the library steps
It is easy to see from the road, so it is safer
A skate park is part of a community
The resident is against young people
questions.explanation: Only this point is about the reserve: the student argues it is open and visible from the road, so it is "safer than the empty car parks". The library steps are another place, and Text 1 says the resident is not against young people skating.

questions.stem: Bee is to hive as bird is to
questions.explanation: A bee lives in a hive and a bird lives in a nest. A flock is a group of birds, not their home.

questions.stem: Which word is closest in meaning to METICULOUS?
questions.explanation: Meticulous means taking great care over every detail, which is thorough. Careless is the opposite.

questions.stem: Which word is most nearly the opposite of TRANSPARENT?
questions.explanation: Transparent means you can see through it, and opaque means you cannot. Clear means nearly the same as transparent.

questions.stem: Which word does not belong with the others?
questions.explanation: The violin, cello and viola are string instruments. The trumpet is a brass instrument.

questions.stem: Which pair comes next? AB, DE, GH, ...
questions.explanation: Each pair is two letters in a row, and one letter is skipped between pairs: AB (C) DE (F) GH (I) JK.

questions.stem: Apton is north of Brill. Corley is south of Brill. Dunmore is north of Apton. Which town is furthest south?
questions.explanation: From north to south the towns are Dunmore, Apton, Brill, Corley.

questions.stem: Every bus on route 9 stops at the library. The bus Sam is on does not stop at the library. Which statement must be true?
options: Sam is not going to the library.
Sam's bus is not on route 9.
No other bus stops at the library.
questions.explanation: A route 9 bus always stops at the library, so a bus that does not stop there cannot be a route 9 bus. Nothing says where Sam wants to go.

questions.stem: Which word means both "a place that keeps people's money" and "the land along the side of a river"?
questions.explanation: A bank looks after money, and a river bank is the land beside a river. Shore is used for the sea or a lake, not a building for money.

questions.stem: Scalpel is to surgeon as easel is to
questions.explanation: A surgeon uses a scalpel and a painter uses an easel. A canvas sits on an easel, but it is not the person who uses it.

questions.stem: Which word is most nearly the opposite of BENEVOLENT?
questions.explanation: Benevolent means kind and wishing others well. Malicious means wanting to cause harm. Generous is close in meaning to benevolent.

questions.stem: Which word does not belong with the others?
questions.explanation: A rectangle, a rhombus and a square each have four sides. A triangle has three.

questions.stem: "The coach was adamant that training would go ahead despite the rain." What does adamant mean in this sentence?
questions.explanation: Adamant means refusing to change your mind. The coach would not be talked out of holding training.

questions.stem: Which letter comes next? C, F, J, O, ...
questions.explanation: The steps grow by one each time: C (+3) F (+4) J (+5) O, so next is +6: O → U.

questions.stem: In a code, each letter is replaced by the letter two places later in the alphabet. What does the code word FQI stand for?
questions.explanation: To decode, move each letter two places back: F→D, Q→O, I→G. HSK moves the letters forward instead.

questions.stem: If BAD is written 214, using each letter's place in the alphabet, how is FACE written?
questions.explanation: F is the 6th letter, A the 1st, C the 3rd and E the 5th, so FACE is 6135.

questions.stem: Some musicians are teachers. All teachers have a degree. Which statement must be true?
options: Everyone with a degree is a teacher.
questions.explanation: The musicians who are teachers must have a degree, so at least some musicians do. The statements say nothing about musicians who are not teachers.

questions.stem: If it rains, the match is cancelled. The match was not cancelled. Which statement must be true?
options: Only rain can cancel the match.
questions.explanation: Rain always leads to a cancellation, so if there was no cancellation there was no rain. The rule does not say rain is the only possible reason for cancelling.

questions.stem: Which word completes both new words? sun___ and ___house
questions.explanation: Sunlight and lighthouse are both words. Sunshine and sunset work, but shinehouse and sethouse do not; greenhouse works, but sungreen does not.

questions.stem: Which word best completes the sentence? "The scientist's explanation was so ___ that even the youngest students could follow it."
questions.explanation: "So ... that even the youngest students could follow it" needs a word meaning clear and easy to understand, which is lucid. Obscure means hard to understand.

questions.stem: Frugal is to spend as taciturn is to
questions.explanation: A frugal person is unwilling to spend much, and a taciturn person is unwilling to speak much.

questions.stem: What is the value of −18 ÷ (−3) − 4 × (−2)?
What is 3/5 − 1/4?
questions.explanation: Use a common denominator of 20: 12/20 − 5/20 = 7/20. 2/9 subtracts the tops and adds the bottoms, which is never allowed.

questions.stem: Increase \$80 by 15%.
questions.explanation: 15% of \$80 is \$12, so the new amount is \$80 + \$12 = \$92. \$68 is a 15% decrease.

questions.stem: A triangle has a base of 16 cm and a perpendicular height of 11 cm. What is its area?
questions.explanation: Area = ½ × base × height = ½ × 16 × 11 = 88 cm². 176 cm² forgets the half.

questions.stem: What is the median of 11, 15, 15, 18, 20, 23 and 26?
questions.explanation: The numbers are already in order and there are seven, so the median is the 4th: 18. 15 is the mode.

questions.stem: Solve 4(x − 3) = 2x + 6.
questions.explanation: Expand: 4x − 12 = 2x + 6. Then 2x = 18, so x = 9. x = 4.5 comes from forgetting to multiply the 3 by 4.

questions.stem: Two angles on a straight line measure (3x + 10)° and (2x + 20)°. What is the value of x?
questions.explanation: Angles on a straight line add to 180°: 5x + 30 = 180, so 5x = 150 and x = 30. Check: 100° + 80° = 180°.

questions.stem: 5 kg of apples costs \$12.50. At the same price per kilogram, how much do 8 kg cost?
A fair spinner is numbered 1 to 8. What is the probability of spinning a prime number?
questions.explanation: The primes from 1 to 8 are 2, 3, 5 and 7, which is 4 of 8 numbers, so 1/2. 1 is not prime, and 2 is the only even prime.

questions.stem: How many 150 mL cups can be filled from a 2.4 L bottle of juice?
What number comes next? 81, 27, 9, 3, ...
questions.explanation: Each number is divided by 3: 3 ÷ 3 = 1.

questions.stem: A number machine multiplies by 4 and then adds 3. The output is 35. What was the input?
questions.explanation: Undo the steps in reverse order: 35 − 3 = 32, then 32 ÷ 4 = 8.

questions.stem: The pairs (2, 7), (5, 16), (8, 25) all follow the same rule. Which number completes (11, ?)?
questions.explanation: The second number is 3 times the first, plus 1: 3 × 11 + 1 = 34. The second number also rises by 9 each time the first rises by 3.

questions.stem: What number comes next? 5, 8, 14, 26, 50, ...
questions.explanation: The gaps double: 3, 6, 12, 24, so the next gap is 48 and 50 + 48 = 98. Another way: double and subtract 2.

questions.stem: The symbol # means m # n = (m + n) ÷ 2. What is the value of (6 # 10) # 4?
4 blocks of type A balance 6 blocks of type B. How many A blocks balance 9 B blocks?
questions.explanation: One A weighs as much as 1.5 B, so 9 B = 9 ÷ 1.5 = 6 A. Check: 6 A is 1.5 times 4 A, and 9 B is 1.5 times 6 B.

questions.stem: Kai is 6 years older than Lena. In 2 years' time their ages will add up to 34. How old is Lena now?
questions.explanation: In 2 years both are 2 older, so their ages now add to 34 − 4 = 30. Lena is (30 − 6) ÷ 2 = 12 and Kai is 18. 14 forgets that both ages grow.

questions.stem: Pens cost \$3 and notebooks cost \$5. Sam buys 8 items and spends exactly \$34. How many notebooks does Sam buy?
questions.explanation: Eight pens would cost \$24. Each notebook instead of a pen adds \$2, and \$34 − \$24 = \$10, so there are 5 notebooks. Check: 5 × \$5 + 3 × \$3 = \$34.

questions.stem: A bus leaves the terminal every 25 minutes, starting at 6:10 am. What is the first bus after 8:00 am?
questions.explanation: The buses leave at 6:10, 6:35, 7:00, 7:25, 7:50 and then 8:15 am.

questions.stem: A 3 by 3 grid is made of 9 small squares. How many squares of any size can be found in it?
questions.explanation: There are 9 small 1 by 1 squares, 4 squares of 2 by 2, and 1 square of 3 by 3: 9 + 4 + 1 = 14.

questions.stem: What is the passage mainly about?
options: How a colony controls the temperature of its nest
How bees turn the nectar they collect into honey
Why bees become aggressive when the weather is hot
How young bees learn to fly and find flowers
questions.explanation: The passage explains why the brood needs steady warmth and how the colony warms and cools the nest.

questions.stem: What do bees do to warm the nest on a cold day?
options: Fan their wings at the nest entrance
Spread droplets of water over the comb
Huddle together and shiver their muscles
Hang in a cluster outside the entrance
questions.explanation: The third paragraph says workers "cluster tightly and shiver their flight muscles". The other actions are for cooling.

questions.stem: Why does spreading water on the comb cool the nest?
options: The water is colder than the air outside
As the water evaporates, it carries heat away
The water stops nectar from heating up
questions.explanation: The passage says that as the water evaporates "it carries heat away", like sweat cooling skin.

questions.stem: "The colony's temperature control emerges from thousands of small decisions." Emerges means
questions.explanation: No single bee is in charge; the control comes about as a result of many bees each reacting. "Is ordered" contradicts "No single bee directs any of this".

questions.stem: How does the writer organise the information about hot days?
options: As a story about one bee
As an argument with two sides
As a list of three methods, in order
As a comparison of bees and ants
questions.explanation: The paragraph uses "First", "Second" and "Third" to set out three ways the colony cools the nest.

questions.stem: Why did Mai let go of Bao's hand?
questions.explanation: She let go "for exactly ten seconds to pay for a showbag".

questions.stem: How does Mai work out where Bao has gone?
options: A stranger points her in the right direction
She hears him calling out her name
She searches every pavilion one by one
She recalls what he had talked about all day
questions.explanation: She decides to "think like Bao" and realises he has talked all day about the tractors.

questions.stem: "The crowd seemed to grow louder and taller." This shows that Mai
options: was standing in a low place
thought the crowd was getting bigger
questions.explanation: The crowd has not really changed. Panic makes it feel bigger and noisier around her.

questions.stem: What does Bao's reaction show about him?
options: The tractor held all his attention
He ran off on purpose to scare Mai
He was frightened and had hidden
He knew Mai would find him quickly
questions.explanation: The story says "He had not even noticed he was lost"; he was staring at the tractor "as if it were a castle".

questions.stem: Why does Mai change her answer from "No" to "Maybe"?
options: She decides Bao is old enough to climb
A farmer nearby has already said yes
Relief makes her want to be kind to him
She wants Bao to stop asking her
questions.explanation: The story says she changed her mind "because her heart was still thumping and she had never been so glad to see anyone in her life".

questions.stem: Puppy is to dog as kid is to
questions.explanation: A puppy is a young dog and a kid is a young goat. A lamb is a young sheep.

questions.stem: Which word is closest in meaning to OBSTINATE?
questions.explanation: Obstinate means refusing to change your mind, so stubborn. Obvious only sounds similar.

questions.stem: Which word is most nearly the opposite of EXPAND?
questions.explanation: To expand is to get bigger and to contract is to get smaller. Grow and stretch are close to expand.

questions.stem: Which word does not belong with the others?
questions.explanation: Sydney, Melbourne and Brisbane are cities. Victoria is a state.

questions.stem: In a code, SHIP is written TIJQ. How is BOAT written in the same code?
questions.explanation: Each letter moves one place forward: S→T, H→I, I→J, P→Q. So B→C, O→P, A→B, T→U. ANZS moves backwards.

questions.stem: Lin is taller than Max. Max is taller than Nia. Oli is shorter than Nia. Who is the shortest?
questions.explanation: From tallest to shortest: Lin, Max, Nia, Oli.

questions.stem: All dolphins are mammals. All mammals breathe air. Which statement must be true?
options: All animals that breathe air are dolphins.
questions.explanation: Every dolphin is a mammal and every mammal breathes air, so every dolphin breathes air. The other statements may be true in real life, but they do not follow from the two given.

questions.stem: Which word best completes the sentence? "The ___ plain had received almost no rain for years."
questions.explanation: A place with almost no rain is dry, which is what arid means. Humid, fertile and lush all suggest plenty of moisture.

questions.stem: Which letter comes next? Z, X, U, Q, ...
questions.explanation: The letters go backwards in steps that grow by one: Z (−2) X (−3) U (−4) Q, so next is −5: Q → L.

questions.stem: Which word can go in front of all three to make new words? ___board, ___cake, ___ful
questions.explanation: Cupboard, cupcake and cupful are all words. Key makes keyboard, hand makes handful and card makes cardboard, but none makes all three.
